ca_tootsie_pop_tower.blurb: A small tower among the Candy Store cluster of knobby spires in the Alabama Hills outside Lone Pine, standing just west of Rock Candy Tower. It holds 13 short routes, most of them set up for top-rope, plus four bolted sport lines and a pair of crack climbs. The grades are friendly: a handful at 5.5 and 5.6, four at 5.9, a few 5.10s and a single 5.11. Lines are brief, some around 50 feet, so it suits a quick warm-up, a first lead on bolts, or a relaxed session with a group of mixed ability.

ca_northwest_face_3.blurb: The northwest side of the Pulpit Rock spire, standing across the river in the Lower Merced River Canyon below Yosemite Valley. It is a steeper, harder wall than most roadside crags: 13 routes, split between trad lines and bolted sport climbs, with nothing easier than 5.10. Expect a few at 5.10, the bulk at 5.11, and a handful at 5.12. The spire is reached only by crossing the Merced, which is practical when the water is low, so it sees fewer parties than the cliffs along the highway.
ca_northwest_face_3.parking_note: Leave the car in the lot at the junction of Highways 140 and 120, then cross the river to reach the spire; the crossing is practical only when the water is very low.

ca_upper_freeway_wall.blurb: The higher of the two Freeway Wall sections, in the Lost Horse Road area of Joshua Tree, reached by following a climber's path into the boulders and scrambling uphill. It is the busier half of the wall and a trad crag at heart: twelve of its 13 routes are placed-gear climbs, with a single top-rope line. Grades run from 5.5 up to 5.10, and about half of them sit at 5.10. The wall looks southwest, so it holds shade in the morning and sun in the afternoon, which makes it a popular winter choice.

ca_watts_towers.blurb: A trad-oriented orange-tinted wall of cracks and dihedrals above the broken domes beside Park Boulevard, in the Hidden Valley part of Joshua Tree. Routes are roughly 50 to 100 feet tall and there are very few bolts, so you build your own anchors and carry a full rack. Of the 13 climbs, twelve are trad and one is a top-rope. The grades cover a wide band from 5.5 to 5.11, with the largest cluster at 5.10. Getting to the base means picking through a jumble of boulders, and the way off is a short, fiddly down-climb.

ca_wimovi_pluton.blurb: A small granite dome in the Shaver Lake area of the southern Sierra, reached by a short use trail along Stevenson Creek not far from Highway 168. The climbing is on its south face, which suits an afternoon of short, punchy routes. Of 13 climbs, eleven are trad and two are sport, with most between 5.8 and 5.10 and one 5.11. The base sits above a waterfall whose flow changes with releases from the lake, so it is a poor choice for unattended children or dogs. The area tends to be quiet.

ca_sullivan_creek.blurb: A mellow bouldering spot of river-polished boulders along a creek drainage off Highway 108, east of Sonora in the Sierra foothills. There are 13 problems, centred on V2 to V4 with one easy V1 and a couple of harder lines at V5 and V7. The style leans toward slabs and vertical faces that end in sloper topouts, with mantels common and a few steeper creek-cut faces. Many boulders stand close to the roadside pullouts with flat landings, so a pad or two is enough. It is a pleasant place to swim between tries when the weather is warm, though poison oak grows along the banks.

ca_vader_roof.blurb: A formation in the Tatooine group of crags on a low hill in the high desert of Apple Valley, west of Jabba, and reached by following the main trail around the left side of the hill. It faces southwest, so it catches the afternoon sun, and shade is scarce across the hill. Mostly bolted: 11 sport routes and two trad lines, spanning 5.7 to 5.10 with one 5.12. Fall through spring is the comfortable season, and the hill is generally quiet, with long views across the dry lake basin.
ca_vader_roof.parking_note: Reach the hill by dirt roads: leave Highway 18 northbound on Joshua Road, turn east onto the unpaved Cahuilla Road, head north up Mountain View Lane, then follow the tracks to the hill. A high-clearance or 4WD vehicle is the safer bet, though careful drivers in 2WD often manage.
